text: Camilla Antoinette Clifford (29 June 1885 – 28 June 1971), known professionally as Camille Clifford, was a Belgian-born stage actress whose brief theatrical career was defined by her performance as "Miss New York" in the Henry W. Savage production of The Prince of Pilsen, a role in which she portrayed a "Gibson Girl"-like woman. Although her towering coiffure and hourglass figure embodied the Gibson Girl style, she only performed the role on stage and never modeled for any of Charles Dana Gibson's illustrations. Clifford was born on 29 June 1885 in Antwerp, Belgium, to Reynold Clifford and Matilda Ottersen, and was raised in Sweden, Norway, and Boston. On 31 August 1903, she made her stage debut as Mazie Manhattan, the New York Girl in "The Song of the Cities," in a Henry W. Savage production of The Prince of Pilsen at the Tremont Theatre in Boston. The role required her to walk across the stage in the style of Charles Dana Gibson's illustrations, leading to a misconception that she was a Gibson model—when in fact, she imitated his work, not the other way around. In early 1904, the Savage company signed a contract with George Musgrove and Frank McKee for a European tour, and to select an actress to join the new "London Company," a contest was held among those who had played Mazie Manhattan; Clifford won and the company departed in late April 1904. Clifford performed in the United States from 1902 and in England from 1904, returning to Boston on 3 July 1906. While typically playing walk-on, non-speaking roles, she gained fame for her beauty and, in the musical show The Catch of the Season, which opened at London's Vaudeville Theatre on 9 September 1904, she sang the song "Sylvia, the Gibson Girl." Her signature style included a long, elegant gown wrapped around a tightly corseted, eighteen-inch wasp waist. She retired from the stage after marrying Captain the Hon. Henry Lyndhurst Bruce (1881–1914), the eldest son and heir apparent of Henry Bruce, 2nd Baron Aberdare, in 1906; they had one child, Margaret, who died five days after birth. Her first husband was killed during the Great War in 1914, and his younger brother, Clarence, succeeded to the barony. In 1917, she married Captain John Meredyth Jones Evans; after the war, she left the stage permanently and later owned a stable of successful racehorses. Together, they were the parents of children, though the specific names are not provided. Her second husband died in 1957, and she died on 28 June 1971. Despite being known as "the quintessential Gibson Girl," she was not the only person to imitate the character on stage or screen. Photographs of her taken by Lizzie Caswall Smith in 1905 are frequently featured in historical fashion books and on websites to illustrate the Edwardian style.
